analysis.one_liner: Lets private investors pay students' college costs in exchange for a share of their future income.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2014 and died there without a vote, cosponsor, or hearing before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make 'income share agreements' legal nationwide. Under such a deal, an investor pays for your college (or job training) now, and in return you owe them a fixed slice of your future paycheck — say, 8% a year for 15 years — no matter how much or how little that adds up to. The bill sets some guardrails: no more than 15% of income can be pledged, the first $10,000 of yearly income is off-limits, and borrowers must get a plain disclosure. But it also overrides state usury laws that cap how much lenders can charge, makes these obligations nondischargeable in bankruptcy, denies students the student-loan interest deduction, and exempts the funds making these deals from investment-company regulation. The bill never got a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries are investors and education-finance companies, who would get a federally sanctioned, federally protected new market: enforceable contracts, freedom from state interest-rate caps, freedom from investment-company regulation, and favorable tax treatment on the money they collect. Students also gain a genuine option — money for school without a fixed dollar debt, and no payments while earning under $10,000 — though what they give up is a long-term claim on their paycheck.

how_it_helps.text: It gives students a way to pay for college or training with no fixed dollar debt: payments rise and fall with income, and nothing is owed on income below $10,000 a year (adjusted for inflation).
It caps what a student can pledge at 15% of future income across all such agreements, and limits the payment period to 30 years (extendable only for years spent below the income exemption).

It requires a clear written disclosure before signing, stating that the agreement is not a debt, that payments may be more or less than the amount received, and that the obligation cannot be wiped out in bankruptcy.
Money received under such an agreement would not count as income or assets when calculating federal financial aid eligibility, so students would not lose grants for using one.

analysis.who_pays: Students who sign pay a fixed share of their paycheck for up to 30 years, and could end up paying far more than they received; they cannot discharge the obligation in bankruptcy and get no student-loan interest deduction. State governments lose their power to cap what these financiers can extract through usury laws, and federal taxpayers absorb the cost of excluding the proceeds from taxable income.
analysis.who_pays_short: Students who sign, and state regulators

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly makes income share obligations nondischargeable in bankruptcy — a protection even federal student loans only partially have — so a signer carries the obligation for life regardless of circumstances.

It preempts state usury laws entirely, so states could not cap the effective price of these agreements, and a high-earning graduate could pay back many multiples of the original funding over up to 30 years.

It exempts companies in the business of making these agreements from the Investment Company Act of 1940, removing a layer of federal investment regulation over the funds that hold students' contracts.

It adds these agreements to the definition of 'qualified education loans' while denying the student-loan interest deduction on payments made under them, so signers get the label without the tax benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students who cannot borrow enough through federal loans — or who fear an unpayable fixed debt — an income share agreement can be a real safety net, and the bill's floor, cap, and disclosure rules are better than nothing. But the design tilts toward the financiers: the obligation lasts up to 30 years, survives bankruptcy, escapes state interest-rate caps, and carries no interest deduction. The bill's core achievement is not student relief but the creation of a legally protected new asset class for investors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Marco Rubio introduced the bill on April 9, 2014, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No cosponsors signed on, and the committee took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State usury laws and investment-company regulation remain intact, and no one is bound to a bankruptcy-proof, 30-year claim on their paycheck under this framework. Investors did not get the new protected market they would have gained, but the status quo lenders and regulators are the ones left better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State regulators and the lending status quo

for.name: Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill to create a federal legal framework for private income share agreements and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on April 9, 2014 and never scheduled a markup or vote, letting it die there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan shape was never tested; the bill died with a single Republican sponsor and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Private education finance and income share agreement investors
industries.note: The bill would hand this industry a federally enforceable new market: freedom from state usury caps, exemption from investment-company regulation, and favorable tax treatment. Its revenue is literally a share of students' future paychecks, though the bill imposes a 15% cap, a $10,000 income floor, and mandatory disclosures.

industries.industry: State governments and their usury/assignment-of-wage laws
industries.note: The bill preempts state usury laws and state limits on assigning future wages, stripping states of their main tools for policing how much these contracts can extract from residents.

Private income share agreements would become an alternative channel for college financing, competing with federal loans, while the bill also excludes their proceeds from financial-aid need calculations so students could stack them on top of federal aid.
